title: The Markovian Thinker
one_liner: Reason in short chunks that keep only a small carried state, so long thinking stays cheap instead of dragging the whole history forward.
lead: Long reasoning is expensive because each new step keeps rereading the entire earlier trace. As that trace grows, cost and memory rise sharply. Delethink changes the process: it writes reasoning in chunks, keeps only a fixed carried state from recent work, and deletes the rest before continuing. This keeps long reasoning practical because each new chunk depends on a bounded summary rather than the full past trace.

problem.h2: Long reasoning gets expensive when every new step carries the full past
paras: A reasoning model often solves a hard problem by generating many intermediate steps. In the usual setup, every new step is computed while keeping the entire earlier trace in memory. If the reasoning trace becomes very long, the model pays for that full history again and again.

That is the core scaling problem. Longer traces can improve difficult tasks because they give the model room to explore more intermediate steps, but the cost of carrying all earlier text rises fast enough to make very long reasoning impractical. Methods that only shorten the trace help somewhat, yet they still tie each new step to the full surviving history because every new step must reread whatever text remains. That keeps the active context growing with whatever text remains, so the cost still rises as the solution gets longer.

callout.html: Break reasoning into chunks and preserve only a fixed carried state between chunks, because the next chunk does not need the whole raw history if the necessary information is summarized well.

steps.text: Generate a bounded segment of reasoning steps.
Keep only a fixed amount of recent or summarized information needed to continue.
Discard the detailed earlier text instead of carrying it forever.
Continue reasoning from the carried state plus the new problem context.

steps.b: Repeat until the problem is solved
steps.text: Chain chunks together so total reasoning can grow while the active memory stays bounded.

paras: The paper changes what gets carried from one reasoning phase to the next. Instead of keeping the entire raw trace, it keeps only a fixed-sized state that is meant to be sufficient for continuation.

hidden.name: how much useful reasoning survives inside the carried state
paras: The hidden quantity is state sufficiency: after deleting most of the old reasoning text, does the carried state still contain what the next chunk needs? If the answer is yes, the model can continue correctly while using much less memory.

Delethink succeeds when the important intermediate facts, goals, and partial conclusions are concentrated inside that carried state. The carried state can be small only if it preserves the information that actually matters for the next step.

heat.caption: Darker cells mark the facts that must survive deletion for reasoning to continue correctly.

reads.html: The small carryover must preserve the real problem-solving state, not just a short snippet of recent text.
The Markovian thinking idea works when a bounded state is sufficient to continue the reasoning process from one chunk to the next.

mechanism.h2: Why chunked reasoning lowers cost without losing ability
paras: Standard long reasoning is expensive because each new chunk is conditioned on the entire earlier trace. That means the active context length keeps growing even if most of the old text no longer matters. The model repeatedly pays to reread details that were only useful earlier.

Delethink breaks this loop. After a chunk is finished, the method retains only a fixed carried state that is meant to summarize the active reasoning situation. The next chunk then conditions on that bounded state. This lowers cost because the active context stops growing with the total reasoning length.

The key bet is that the reasoning process has a local state: what subgoal is active, what conclusions have already been established, and what constraints still matter. If those essentials fit into the carried state, deleting the old raw prose does not hurt much. The model gets long total reasoning while the active context remains small.

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose chunk 1 proves that quantity A equals quantity B and that only case 2 remains.
The carried state keeps two facts: 'A = B' and 'active case = 2'.
The full raw text of chunk 1 is deleted.
Chunk 2 starts from those two carried facts and derives the final answer.
This works because chunk 2 needed the established equality and the active case, not every sentence from chunk 1.

math.note: The method lives or dies by whether the carried state is sufficient for continuation.

charts.title: Carry the full reasoning history
charts.note: As the trace grows, cost rises because every new step keeps rereading the whole past.

charts.title: Chunked carried-state reasoning
charts.note: The active context stays fixed, so long reasoning becomes practical at much lower cost because each new chunk no longer rereads the entire earlier trace.

items.html: If the carried state misses a key fact or active constraint, the next chunk may continue from an incomplete problem state and drift into wrong reasoning.
A proof or program synthesis task may depend on a small detail from much earlier text, and a fixed carried state may not preserve it unless the summarization is careful.
If a chunk ends in the middle of a delicate argument, the carried state may need to encode that unfinished state precisely or the next chunk will lose continuity.
When the carried state captures the live subgoal, established facts, and remaining constraints, deleting old prose saves cost because the next chunk no longer needs the full earlier wording.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Take a reasoning benchmark with long step-by-step solutions and compare two versions of the same model: one that carries the full trace and one that uses carried-state chunking. Hold the maximum active context fixed. Measure solve rate, memory use, and total generated reasoning length before failure.
demo.closing: The demo should show that chunked carried-state reasoning can keep solving hard problems after the full-history version hits its memory wall, because the active context remains bounded even when total reasoning grows long.
